summary:
Futucropper is a free web app that tells farmers where and when to sow, using 23 years of NASA satellite data. Our team is three students from Ukraine and two from Australia, and we started with one shared problem: farms in the world’s breadbaskets are losing the water they depend on, while farming itself adds to the warming that makes drought worse. In southern Ukraine, the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in 2023 left the largest irrigation system dry. In Australia’s Murrumbidgee, the 2018–19 drought cut the water farmers could use. The causes differ, but the result is the same, so we built one solution for both.

The app combines MODIS vegetation, GPM IMERG rainfall, GLDAS soil moisture and MERRA-2 temperature. A map shows where the land is best and when to sow. A field plan gives a risk score for a crop and month, seed amount, the field’s emissions with ways to cut them, and a season plan. A timeline shows how the land has changed since 2003 and where trends point by 2035. A weather-only model separates damage caused by people (the lost dam water) from damage caused by drought. An AI assistant explains the results in five languages using only the app’s numbers.

Farmers can’t use raw satellite files. Futucropper turns two decades of them into decisions a farmer can act on, and shows how farming can heat the climate less. We built it across two countries because we only have one Earth to share.
details:
Futucropper is a free web and Android app that turns 23 years of NASA satellite data (2003–2025) into farming decisions. A map shows where the land is best and when to sow. A field plan gives a risk score for a chosen crop and month, the reasons behind it, seed amount, a step-by-step season guide, and the field's greenhouse gas emissions with ways to cut them. A timeline shows how the land changed season by season since 2003 and where trends point by 2035. A weather-only model separates damage caused by people, such as the lost Kakhovka dam water, from damage caused by drought. An AI assistant explains the results in five languages using only the app's numbers.

Benefits: One free tool replaces four separate ones (satellite map, weather service, agronomy guide, emissions calculator). Farmers can test a plan before spending money on seed, fertiliser, fuel and water. It works on a phone, offline on Android, and in English, Ukrainian, German, French and Italian.

Intended impact: Fewer failed harvests and lower emissions, one field at a time. We focused on southern Ukraine, where about 243,600 ha of irrigated land lost water after the Kakhovka dam was destroyed, and Australia's Murrumbidgee, where water allocation fell to 7% in the 2018–19 drought. Because NASA data is global, the method can be extended to any farming region.

Tools: NASA MODIS, GPM IMERG, GLDAS, MERRA-2 and GIBS; NOAA, World Bank, IPCC and FAO data. Python (FastAPI, pandas, scikit-learn), TypeScript (Next.js, React, Leaflet, Recharts), Jupyter, GitHub, Render and Vercel, an Android build with offline mode, an AI model via OpenRouter, and Claude for coding help. No special hardware.

Why it is creative: It joins three questions other tools keep apart: is my plan risky, what does it emit, and how will this land change. It also shows why fields suffer, people or weather, not just that they do. And one method works for two opposite cases, war and drought, built by a team of three Ukrainians and two Australians.

Factors we considered: Honesty about uncertainty. The score is a comparison, not a harvest probability. Emissions are estimates. Future years are scenarios, not forecasts, and forecasts that failed tests are hidden. The AI never invents numbers. We also considered different water situations in each country, local agronomy advice, and access for farmers with weak internet.
